task.name: hardening: enforce per-test timeouts in gate runs
task.story_text:
CONVENTIONS.md states that every test must complete in under five seconds and
that no test may perform blocking I/O without a timeout. Nothing enforces it. The
rule is advisory prose, so a test that violates it is discovered only when it
consumes an entire gate run.

When that happens the gate's verdict carries no attribution. The suite is killed as
a whole, so the run ends without a complete verdict and without naming the test
that consumed the budget. Whatever the log happens to show before the kill — some
assertion failures, the termination line — the one thing it cannot supply is which
test was responsible, and whether it was slow or genuinely blocked.

## Why

Re-evidenced on 2026-08-29. A sprint on #2681 cycled through repeated DEV
iterations without ever establishing whether the branch's tests passed: a newly
added production wait caused pre-existing, previously-compliant coordinator tests
to block, and the suite was terminated past ten minutes with no summary. The
absence of a named culprit then produced competing reconstructions of the failure,
none of which the artifacts could settle quickly.

The bound cannot be enforced by asking developers to honour it. The tests that
blocked here were not written in violation of the rule — they were compliant when
written, and a change elsewhere in the tree made them slow. No authoring-time
discipline reaches that case; only an enforced budget does.

## Scope

Enforcing the bound exposes pre-existing tests that already violate the five-second
rule. Bringing those tests under the bound while preserving their coverage is **in
scope for this story** — they are directly related to it, and the general prohibition
on modifying existing tests unrelated to a story does not apply to them.

The remedy is to make them faster. No test is skipped, excluded from the default
gate, moved behind a marker, or granted a longer bound to get the suite green. If a
specific test cannot be brought under the bound without losing coverage, stop and
report that test and why, rather than working around it.

## Acceptance criteria

- The test configuration checked into the repository declares a per-test time bound
  matching the documented five-second rule, and whatever the runner needs in order
  to enforce it is a declared development dependency rather than an assumption
  about the environment.
- The bound is declared once, in configuration, so that every invocation of the
  suite inherits it without a flag being passed — the project gate, the developer
  check, and a bare runner invocation in a terminal alike. An invocation nobody
  anticipated inherits the bound rather than escaping it.
- A test that blocks past the bound is named in the run's output together with a
  stack trace locating where it was stuck, so the run's failure is attributable
  rather than anonymous. A deterministic test demonstrates this using its own short
  bound, so the demonstration does not add the default bound's duration to every
  run.
- The baseline suite remains green under enforcement without skips, broad
  exclusions, or widening the shared bound.
- A per-test override may shorten the bound — for example, for a deterministic test
  that proves the enforcement works. No test in the default suite may raise it
  above the shared five-second bound; validation that legitimately needs longer
  belongs outside the default gate.

## Example

Today, a coordinator test that blocks on a real polling path ends the run like this
— no test name, no stack trace, no exit status:

```
........................................F...............   [ 91%]
make: *** [dev-check] Terminated: 15
```

Afterwards the same test should be named as having exceeded the bound, with a stack
trace showing where it was stuck, so the failure is attributable to it rather than
to the run as a whole.

## Observed on the two failed attempts (measured 2026-08-30)

Both dev iterations implemented the bound and both deadlocked the suite. Direct
measurements on an idle machine:

- Base branch `make gate`: **92s** wall clock, 10,296 passed, 0 failed.
- With enforcement configured as `timeout = 5` / `timeout_method = "signal"` under
  `[tool.pytest.ini_options]`, alongside the pre-existing
  `addopts = "-n auto --dist worksteal"`: the run reaches ~99%, stops, and never
  finishes — still running past **600s**, versus 92s green on base.
- At that point all ten xdist workers are alive at **0.0% CPU**. Sampling one shows
  its main thread parked acquiring a lock, and its execnet receiver thread blocked
  reading from the master:

```
main-thread
  ... method_vectorcall_VARARGS_KEYWORDS
        lock_PyThread_acquire_lock
          acquire_timed
            PyThread_acquire_lock_timed      <-- parked here indefinitely

receiver thread
  _io__Buffered_read -> _bufferedreader_raw_read -> _io_FileIO_readinto
    -> _Py_read -> read
```

Zero CPU across every worker distinguishes this from a slow suite: nothing is
executing, and nothing will wake up. The gate reports only
`TIMEOUT after 360s: make gate`, so neither iteration was ever shown this.

Related hazard already recorded in CONVENTIONS.md: forked xdist workers that inherit
a held lock deadlock. This is evidence of what happens, not a prescription for which
enforcement mechanism to use.

events.undefined_case: Four tests remain over the bound, and the cost is not in the tests. Measured on test_protected_base_parallel_merge_pr_poc (3.06s serial, over 5s only under the gate's -n auto parallelism): 29% is forge's own per-spawn process supervision (a bare `git --version` is 3.5ms; through _run_shell it is 7.8ms, i.e. 4.11ms x 219 spawns), and that overhead grows with the host process table (5.93ms to 9.89ms with 200 extra processes) while plain git stays flat — so under 32 concurrent workers every worker pays an inflated version of it at once. A further 39% is memory publication, spread flat across many small git calls whose cadence these tests exist to assert. The tests' own fixtures are already lean: 113 of 137 spawns in the smallest failing test come from production sprint code, only 11 from the test. The Scope section says the remedy is to make the tests faster, but there is no remaining test-side waste; the only lever that would close the gap is reducing the three per-spawn process-table scans in process_group/process_tree, which #2309 added deliberately as defense-in-depth (one for descendants of a short-lived command, one for late descendants, one for setsid escapees). The criterion and Scope do not say whether trading that containment margin for test speed is an acceptable remedy, and it is a materially different kind of change from making a test faster — a subtle regression there means orphaned agent processes in production, which is the exact failure that machinery prevents, and it is not a failure these tests would reliably catch.
events.assumption: I will not modify the containment machinery. I will leave process_group/process_tree scanning exactly as it is and report these four tests as unable to meet the bound without either losing the coverage they exist for or reducing that containment margin: test_protected_base_parallel_merge_pr_poc (3.06s), test_assignment_history_learning_end_to_end (2.53s), test_a_reachable_refusal_is_prevented_by_the_publication_seam (1.93s), test_a_non_landing_workflow_is_unaffected (1.62s). Everything else this story fixed stays as landed.
options_considered: Treat reducing per-spawn supervision overhead as in scope: share one process-table snapshot between the tracker's final observe and the lease sweep at release, cutting three scans to two. Contained and roughly 10% on these tests, but it makes the second consumer read a fractionally older snapshot, which is a small widening of the escapee window.

Go further and make the whole per-spawn scan cheaper with a single bulk read, which #2309 cycle 4 explicitly rejected because its fallback silently degraded back to the full scan. Largest payoff, and it re-opens a settled design decision.

Accept that these four tests cannot meet the bound as written and address them in a separate story that restructures them into narrower tests not each driving a full sprint over real git — keeping enforcement as landed and the gate red on this family until then.

Leave the tests and the machinery alone and reduce gate parallelism instead, since the tests pass serially at 1.6-3.1s and only fail under -n auto oversubscription. The plan explicitly told me not to change Makefile commands, so I have not.

'Make them faster' in the Scope section includes redesigning a test that drives a full sprint over real git into narrower tests asserting the same behaviour without that cost. No remaining waste inside the current design is not the same as that design being required. Do not touch the process_group/process_tree containment machinery: the margin #2309 bought is not available to trade for test speed, and these tests would not reliably catch a regression in it. Do not change gate parallelism, and do not skip, exclude, mark, or widen the bound. handoff.summary: I attempted the directed restructuring and established that it cannot reach the bound, with the specific blocking assertion identified per test. Two structural findings closed it out. First, splitting these tests into narrower ones does not reduce the maximum duration: pytest-timeout runs with func_only=False, so the timer is armed in pytest_runtest_protocol and covers the setup phase, meaning a sprint moved into a module-scoped fixture is still charged to whichever test triggers it — one test at 3.06s plus four at 0.01s, gate result unchanged. Second, I traced the per-spawn cost to source and it is exactly the machinery I was told not to touch: _run_shell_detailed (util.py:560-592) calls register_agent_group, starts a descendant_tracker, and releases through the lease sweep, which is the 4.3ms/spawn gap between a bare `git --version` at 3.5ms and the same command through _run_shell at 7.8ms. In test_a_non_landing_workflow_is_unaffected, 81 of 113 spawns are memory publication (1.14s of 1.48s subprocess time), running five full publish cycles for a two-story sprint. So any design that drives the scheduler pays containment overhead times spawn count, and the four remaining tests each have at least one assertion that is a run outcome rather than a mechanism: scheduler admission ordering, specs_succeeded, a two-halved counterfactual, and learning accumulated across successive runs. I made no code changes rather than ship a risky partial edit to delicate seam tests for roughly 7% — the test-side share of test_protected_base_parallel_merge_pr_poc is 53 of 219 spawns, and eliminating most of it lands at about 2.85s, still failing. Tree is clean and lint green at 47f370b3.

deferred_items: FINDING FOR ITS OWN STORY, as directed: forge's per-spawn process supervision costs 4.11ms on top of the command itself — a bare `git --version` is 3.51ms, the same command through _run_shell is 7.82ms — and that overhead grows with the host process table (5.93ms with an idle machine, 9.89ms with 200 extra processes) while plain subprocess cost stays flat at ~3.5ms. The source is util.py:560-592: register_agent_group, descendant_tracker(...).start(), and the release-time lease sweep, i.e. three process-table scans per spawn covering three distinct blind spots from #2309. Under a 32-worker gate every worker pays an inflated version simultaneously, so the cost is superlinear in test parallelism. For a sprint test making 219 supervised spawns that is 0.90s idle and roughly double under load. Worth its own story; not touched here.

Four tests remain over the bound under gate parallelism while passing serially: test_protected_base_parallel_merge_pr_poc (3.06s), test_assignment_history_learning_end_to_end (2.53s), test_a_reachable_refusal_is_prevented_by_the_publication_seam (1.93s), test_a_non_landing_workflow_is_unaffected (1.62s). Each has at least one assertion that is a run outcome rather than a mechanism, named individually under the baseline-green criterion above.

Memory publication runs five full publish cycles (fetch, worktree add, commit, worktree remove, prune) for a two-story sprint — 81 of 113 spawns in the smallest failing test. Whether that cadence is necessary is a production question these tests assert the timing of, so it was not changed; it may be worth examining alongside the supervision finding.

Tests that skip locally but run on the gate are a standing blind spot for duration work: 38 skip locally against 29 on the gate, which is why the sandboxed group-kill test was over budget by construction and only the gate revealed it.

handoff.summary: Two of the four remaining failures turned out to be fixable, which corrects my previous cycle's conclusion that all four were irreducible. First, test_records_a_grandchild_that_left_the_group was a race rather than a duration problem: the child held the parent link for a fixed time.sleep(2) while the test waited for the tracker to record a setsid'd grandchild through it, so under load two interpreter startups plus the tracker's first 50ms sample can outlast the hold, the child exits, the grandchild reparents, and the assertion fails for want of the link. It runs in 0.08s serially and still failed the gate. acceptance_criteria.criterion: The baseline suite remains green under enforcement without skips, broad exclusions, or widening the shared bound.
acceptance_criteria.notes: No skips, exclusions, re-marking, or widening anywhere. Gate went 25 to 13 to 7 to 4 to 3 to 2 and now oscillates 2-4 with run duration. Three candidate hot spots were measured and rejected this story: the lease sweep at 8%, gh at 0.03s, and thread creation at ~0ms. acceptance_criteria.criterion: A per-test override may shorten the bound — for example, for a deterministic test that proves the enforcement works. No test in the default suite may raise it above the shared five-second bound; validation that legitimately needs longer belongs outside the default gate.
acceptance_criteria.notes: validate_timeout_mark accepts shorter numeric overrides (positional and keyword) and rejects timeout(6), timeout(timeout=6), timeout(0), negative values, method=/timeout_method= (keyword and positional), func_only=True, and non-numeric or bool values without crashing collection. Marks are read via iter_markers so module-level pytestmark and parametrized marks are covered. Violations are stashed at collection and raised as a named failure at setup rather than as a collection-time exception, because under xdist collection runs in the workers where raising would crash the worker instead of naming the test.

Correction to my earlier note: the process-table scan measures 1.6ms and thread creation measures ~0ms, so scans are the largest single component at roughly half the total, with the remainder in sidecar write, lease sweep and fork/exec bookkeeping. Do not chase thread creation.

FINDING, worth its own story: a memory publish that has nothing to commit costs 12-14 subprocess spawns to discover it, reaching the 'Everything staged is already on the memory branch' branch at memory_publication.py:414-420 only after git fetch, git worktree add, a copy, git add --force and an empty git status — 26 spawns and 346ms over a two-story sprint. An earlier experiment showed why it accumulates: with the publish stubbed, staging is never pruned and a test slowed 3.5x. A sound in-process memo is available (skip the worktree when the resolved start-point sha and the staged files' content hashes are both unchanged since the last CLEAN verdict), which avoids the mode and filter subtleties of comparing against git blobs directly.

Tests racing a fixed window rather than exceeding a budget remain a distinct fragility class worth a sweep: test_records_a_grandchild_that_left_the_group ran in 0.08s serially and still failed the gate because its 2s parent-link hold closed under load. That instance is fixed. test_a_story_refused_before_integration_does_not_refuse_its_siblings holds a story open on a 60s Event wait, which would blow the bound outright if the story it waits for were ever not dispatched.
